utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Alex Demirdjian; Thomas Laugel; legal intern, Ljubica Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukcevic. May I remind that you're still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukcevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On Thursday, we left it off with you talking about the negotiations with the HDZ in 1990, in the month of August of that year. The representative of the HDZ was Mr. Vekic. I would now like to show you some proposals that you prepared which were subsequently published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D3744. It is 1D3744.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't have tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember this text or, rather, this article on the right-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember it because I wrote it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can remember, there are eight proposals here. You had drafted them on behalf of the SDS. Let's talk about proposal number 1. You say: "We propose that the implementation of a demand reminiscent of Fascist behaviour, by the citizens of Sibenik ..." I am repeating because this has not been recorded. "... to expel or drive out --"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... reminiscent of Fascist behaviour ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Dr. Raskovic, SDS president; Branko Popovic, SDS general secretary; and Marko Dobrijevic, SDS executive committee member, to be stopped in an appropriate but firm manner, and that the decision terminating their employment because they failed to return on time from their annual leave be annulled." And you also say that it is against common sense to expel somebody out of a city where they live and work and especially if they want to return to the city from which they had been expelled after the annual leave. Finally, you cite the provisions of the constitution which indicate that this decision is against the law. What kind of decision are you talking about? What did the citizens of Sibenik decide? How come that these three people were expelled from that city?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details of that decision. However, it was a time when a little spark could cause a forest fire which spread really quickly. An atmosphere of intolerance was created. Reasons were being sought to blame people, to accuse them of things, to engage in illegal and bad behaviour. And then, based on that, if things were established to be as they were purported to be - and I'm talking about the accusations against the Serbs - the awareness was created about the Serbs that they were a destructive, evil people who had to be blamed for all the misfortune and hardship of the Croatian people. The three people in question, of whom two were natives of Sibenik, while Professor Jovan Raskovic also spent his entire life in that city, were supposed to be condemned after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As we are reading this text, we see that you say in it - and this has not been recorded - you say that this had to be prevented in an appropriate and decisive manner. Could you please tell us what you referred to, what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted people to stop talking, that they should be expelled from the city. I wanted them to start saying that they should stay living in the city where they had lived up to then. As you can see, and as can you read, I am referring to article 259, paragraph 1, of the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, which is a legacy of the civilisation and law contained in all the constitutions of the world. According to that article, the citizens are guaranteed freedom of movement and establishment of residence. I had the right to move and live where I see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more question about that. That demand on behalf of the citizens of Sibenik for the three Serbs in question to be expelled from that city, how was it received among the Serbs, not only in Sibenik but in the general area?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the first such extreme cases. Obviously they confused every normal person who didn't even have to be a Serb. They couldn't understand how things like that could happen so many years after the Fascist rule had reigned. Obviously the Serbian Democratic Party as an organisation aimed at protecting the interests and positions of the Serbs in Croatia felt to have been put on spot. They felt the need to protect the individuals belonging to their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more question about this. Dr. Raskovic, Branko Popovic and Marko Dobrijevic, did they remain living in Sibenik or did they have to leave it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under 6, you requested that the legality and legitimacy of the Serbian plebiscite should be recognised. What plebiscite are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Thursday I spoke about the plebiscite and referendum and I emphasised that I had insisted on the referendum not being organised but, rather, that a plebiscite should be organised which was a more democratic form of decision-making. Its aim was to look at all the things that were happening during the turbulent times and to legalize them in a certain way, in a democratic way, to show that it was not a will of a mere few individuals but the will of the entire people, and I mean the Serbian people. You will understand that this was of real interest, and this was the desire of every political factor and every political people in all countries and in all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the question asked at this plebiscite where the Serbian people had to declare themselves?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian people declared that they wish and demand, and here I have to draw your attention to the fact that Serbs wanted and were defending a country called Yugoslavia from any attempt, especially the attempts of Croatia and the Croatian new ideology, to eliminate that country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, could you please focus on the question Mr. Zivanovic put to you. Mr. Zivanovic asked what the question was in the plebiscite. What question did people have to respond to by a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs wanted cultural autonomy, the use of their language and script in Croatia in the event that Croatia should stay within Yugoslavia. If Croatia were to separate from Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, do you remember what the question was in the plebiscite? Was it one question? Were there many questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what were the two questions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish culture autonomy if Croatia remains within Yugoslavia? And if Croatia should secede, do you want political autonomy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At this plebiscite, was the question ever asked whether, in the event Croatia should secede, Serbs wished to stay within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did Serbs want to remain within Yugoslavia? We didn't ask that question, but we knew they wanted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 7, you asked for elections that would enable the Serbian people to independently propose and elect their own representatives within the Croatian parliament. Was this proposal accepted?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the proposals that are before you was accepted, and none of them was given due consideration. It is curious that this particular proposal you mentioned under number 7 was decided upon in the way that I proposed only ten years later, when Croatia adopted the Law on the National List. There was the state list that you receive in the ballot box, and you receive the national list, exactly as I proposed and demanded, to choose from the national list the person you want to represent you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you know a person known as Borivoje Savic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about these proposals and at the negotiations with Mr. Vekic, was Borivoje Savic the one who decided that these negotiations should be conducted?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Borivoje Savic perhaps prepare you for these talks and how you should engage in them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he send you to Dr. Raskovic in Sibenik for consultations, maybe?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Main Board ex officio because you said you were the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS for Baranja?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the province, yes, ex officio, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Goran Hadzic a member of that Main Board?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us if you attended the meeting of the Main Board of the SDS in Lapac in February 1992; and, if you did, tell us what happened there.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met there so that the highest officials of the party could state their position as to whether we were going to follow the course charted by Milosevic for us, through his representatives, or we were going to show that we were aware we were living in a different area in which we were not alone. Milan Babic was in the faction that was spurred on by Milosevic, but the number of people opposed to him, opposed to that faction, was constantly growing. We voted on that occasion, and Milan Babic, with several of his faithful followers, lost this vote. He was defeated. He was defeated by the Serbs, and it really happened the way I'm telling you. If you allow me to explain it a little more. Those who defeated Milan Babic and his faction were the Serbs who wanted to peacefully co-exist with Croats and who believed that it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document on the screen. It is 1D2401.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not object to the admissibility of the proposals. However, this is published in a newspaper article and we have a -- I believe what is the original on tab 3 of the Prosecution list. I will also be using it in cross-examination. I'm wondering, in order to avoid duplication, whether it would make sense to have the original. And perhaps if my learned friend wishes to do so, he can display it on the screen now to ensure that Mr. Vukcevic agrees that this is the proposals he made. The 65 ter is 6576 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed this document on the Prosecution list, and it is absolutely the same as the document published in this article, newspaper article. I don't object if this document would be tendered instead of the one that we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's admit the original then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If it was original, I'm not very -- if it was original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the photograph from the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We need to go to page 2. This is not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the other pages because the proposal had the eight items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Seven, eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it -- however, I would ask just two pages of this document to be admitted because the first page is not -- is not the proposals of Mr. Vukcevic. And in that case, I would -- if not, I would ask the tendering of this document that I used for cross -- for the direct examination of Mr. Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can remove the first page, Your Honours, and solve this during the break with Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's do that. So you'll come back to us. Okay, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, at this meeting in Donji Lapac, did Goran Hadzic also attend?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what he voted for, what he favoured?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic was always in favour of peacefully co-existing with the Croats, avoiding conflict, preferring negotiations and talks and agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D3745.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a tab number, please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, sorry. It is tab 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember this article on the screen, the newspaper articling titled: "Who Shot" -- "Who Fired at the House of V. Vukcevic." Is it about your house?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is about my house. I am the one whose house was fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the subheading, we see that, according to the unofficial version, it was discontented members of the SDS who fired at the house. Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the early days of the Serbian movement in Croatia, there were two factions: One that wanted a humane and proper agreement with majority people, the Croatian people; and another faction that stood in its way. This second faction was supported by people close to Milosevic. This brave Serb who, in the small hours, parked his car outside my house and fired through the window at a room upstairs was from the ranks of this second faction, and the immediate reason for that was precisely the meeting in Donji Lapac, where Milan Babic and his faction, the faction that he led and spoke for, was defeated. And the people who were in the car with the shooter knew that I belonged to the other side and that I advocated negotiations and talks with Croatia. So to punish me for that, they fired at my house. That night the telephone rang, and my wife answered and a voice said, "This time we fired at your house. The next time we will fire at your head." I was still not at home that night. I was not able to drive because of bad weather, and I stayed that night at the hotel, but the next day when I came home, I heard what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this happened immediately after the meeting in Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it happened the night after the meeting, because the news that the faction of Milan Babic was defeated and that the people around him, the people who were representing that option, were losing their positions and losing their importance came after the meeting, and they wanted to remain important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember and did you attend the meeting of the Main Board of the SDS in Obrovac in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting of the Executive Board of the SDS. Yes, I attended that meeting. It was the Saturday of the Catholic Easter 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that just after that Borivoje Savic and Goran Hadzic were arrested at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We left the meeting in small groups or one by one, and so Boro Savic, Goran Hadzic and I found ourselves in the street together. They were close friends of mine and I invited them to come to Beograd on the sea and spend that night at my apartment to rest before the trip that was ahead of us. However, they said they couldn't because the next morning they had to be in Vukovar; they already had commitments. So I remember very well every detail about that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document from the screen into evidence. Sorry, I'll repeat. I would tender the document from the screen into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D3746. It is tab 12. Would you move the original text to the left. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukcevic, you will see here a newspaper story from Politika of 31 April 1991 speaking about the situation in Borovo Selo. It was a time when Savic and Hadzic were in prison. I had not ask you about it, but I want you to look at the box on the right-hand side where it says, "Vukcevic may not represent us." You will see it now enlarged on the screen so you can read it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, and I have it in my collection of documents. Yes. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Are you aware that, on the 1st of April or perhaps the day before, on the 31st of March, such a decision was made that you may not be a representative?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about it from the newspapers, like everyone else. Of course, that decision was not possible. It was impossible to make that decision there. There was a body above the body indicated on the screen that had decided that I would be the only authorised representative of the Serbian community with the Croatian Democratic Union and only the Executive Board could repeal that decision. Certainly a local body could not repeal it. And what we see here is a local body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in Beli Manastir at the time when the armed conflict in Croatia had already begun. Can you tell us if the municipality of Beli Manastir had taken any steps to prevent this conflict? Tell us briefly and then we will look at a document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beli Manastir is a relatively small place, small town. It has the status of a town in a part of Croatia which historically is a province called Baranja. The population is made up of three communities: Serbs, Croats, and Hungarians. There was a fourth group that declared themselves as Yugoslav. Unfortunately, or fortunately, they were not recognised after the time we are discussing as Yugoslavs. They were required to declare themselves as Serbs, Croat, or Hungarians. None of this was accepted. People were very distrustful, had a lot of misgivings. The parliament was elected from all the three, or, let's say, four communities, including the Yugoslavs, and every representative wrote his ethnicity next to his name. There was a total of 250 of them. That parliament, such as it was, adopted a decision to oppose any change of border, any change at all, in the territory of Yugoslavia, a decision that Baranja was part of Yugoslavia and would remain so and would oppose any change. That is the environment in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honours, I'm looking at the 65 ter summary provided for Dr. Vukcevic, and this subject and this line of question is not included at all, nor is it included in the 92 ter statement. So, on that basis, we have no notice that any questions are expected in relation to the situation in Beli Manastir or any measures to prevent the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. However, during the proofing with Mr. Vukcevic, I got one document - it is a one-page document - about the situation in Beli Manastir on 3rd of July, 1991, and the decisions of the municipal assembly related to the situation. I informed the Prosecution in the form of proofing notes about this document and my intention to use this document. I put it both on our amended Rule 65 ter list and the document was on our Defence list for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I inquire: Are the questions going to be limited to this one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In that case then, I withdrew my objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D3747. It is tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukcevic, I believe that you have that text in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's first look at the text on the left-hand side of the screen or, rather, the first column in the B/C/S text headed, "Conclusion." I'm interested in the second sentence which reads: "Fear and distrust have led to the emigration of children, women, even whole families, and almost every village is organising some sort of self-defence." Did you find it? In the first paragraph under "Conclusion"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second sentence --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I've got it, "Fear and distrust," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: When it comes to this sentence, does it faithfully reflect the situation in Baranja at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, the sentiment changed from one village to the next, from one environment to the next. In one village, there were people who really did move out, and in another village, there were people who prevented such behaviour and they were saying that there was no need to move out because nothing would happen to anybody. In any case, the general sentiment and the general state of affairs was that of sickness of abnormality and one would say that it sooner reflected this. I repeat: There were 250 members of the local parliament, including members of all the peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the second paragraph and read the last sentence in it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence which reads: "Unlike the earlier assembly structure, the present composition of the assembly has no powers over the MUP, the judiciary, the prosecutor's office ... "

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The health care, the secondary education," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to invite your comment on just one thing. What does this mean? What does it mean that the present composition has no powers over the MUP and the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should use a few words. I don't know whether I may be allowed to use a lot of words. The election in Croatia was in 1992 and the document was drafted in 1991. As soon as they took power, the HDZ and its representatives, they instilled changes in the organisation of powers. Up to then I was the president of the court in Beli Manastir. And up to then, us judges and the president of the court were either elected or appointed or nominated by the local parliament. As of April 1990 that practice stopped. The state took over in order to be able to control the election of people into various positions, and so on and so forth. In the space of just one year, from April 1990 to July 1991, when this conclusion was issued, many changes had taken place. However, despite that, among the people, there was still the awareness, the desire and the need to live together. That is a fact. There's no two ways about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, I would also kindly ask you to look at the other document on the same page, and this is the amendments to the resolution on the peaceful co-existence of the citizens of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to next page of the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've told us that the municipal assembly of Baranja made the decision that the borders should not be changed. Could you please look at the text of the document --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and can you tell us whether this was the document that established that the borders shouldn't be changed, as you have just told us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand that I have to go back to the fact that this was a decision issued by the local parliament and that the local parliament had been elected directly by all those who had the right to vote, and that the local parliament encompassed representatives of all the three peoples. Even a year into the HDZ rule in Croatia, they still managed to decide that the borders shouldn't be changed, that Baranja should be part of Croatia and that Croatia should be part of Yugoslavia and that they didn't want those facts and that community to be altered in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time on the eve of the clashes and during the clashes, you had plenty of opportunities to listen to the statements given by the politicians on both sides. We've also had opportunities to hear verbal threats addressed at each other. First of all, tell us whether such statements were typical of only one side, or the other side, or of both sides?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a time when people behaved aggressively. Their conscience was distorted. It was a crazy time. One didn't know whether you would wake up in the morning, having gone to bed the previous night. Both sides, unfortunately, were equally mad. The less numerous ones that I belonged to tried and fought hard to adhere to the form of consciousness that had existed and persisted from the end of the Second World War, and that was the awareness of the importance of a community; whereas, those who were more numerous were very, very aggressive. It was painful. You can't even begin to understand how terrible that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You communicated with Goran Hadzic. How well did you know him? What did you think of him and his behaviour under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met quite often. We often travelled together. Whenever we went to the meeting of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, which usually took place in Knin, and that was 650 kilometres away from the cities where we lived. We travelled together, and during such long journeys we talked about all sorts of things. I know Goran's family. I know where he was born, his social environment, where he grew up. It was a very tame environment, a very regular family, and nobody who hailed from that family could even have dirty shoes, let alone something bad on his mind. There was a lot of order in that family, so there could be nothing disorderly about anybody who hailed from such a family. He was well nurtured. He was well fed, well clothed. He had everything that he needed in life. He could not be spiteful, he could not be evil, he could not be a bad man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, just one more question for you. You said that there was a stream that strongly advocated co-existence with Croats and there was another stream which -- where would you classify Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly put him among those of us who wanted to live together with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, after all the developments, in hindsight, that desire for Croats and Serbs to live together in Croatia, has that materialised?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very hard to talk about other people's opinions about other people's fortunes or misfortunes. Everyone can speak for themselves. However, from what one hears and from what one knows, things as they are now are a far cry from what they used to be before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukcevic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I begin my cross-examination, the document that we were exchanging about earlier has been altered in order to be admitted now. It's 65 ter 6576 if we want have it displayed just for Mr. Zivanovic's assurance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It seems that I did not ask the tendering of the last document and I would do it now, and apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is it 1D3747?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is document 3747, 1D.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Exhibit D185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Maybe we'll deal with that document with Mr. Zivanovic during the break to save court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We haven't met before. My name is Alex Demirdjian, and I will have some questions for you this morning on behalf of the Prosecution. And if at any time my questions are not clear, please don't hesitate to ask me for clarification. Let me begin with where you just left off with respect to Mr. Hadzic. In your statement you stated that: "Until I left the SDS in April 1991, Goran Hadzic was in the moderate wing of the SDS." Are you suggesting that this changed after April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, the decision was made which denied me the right to represent the Serbian people in Croatia. It was a very aggressive and a not-well-thought-through decision made by certain individuals, but it was a watershed for counting the time before and after. I don't know if I made myself clear. On the 1st of April, that is, a decision was made to deprive me of that right, and they did it because they knew that I was a peace-loving person and that I could not represent their aggressive behaviour and their aggressive positions. In that case, the period up to the 1st of April is one kind of time, and after that, another kind of time. I don't know if I'm making myself clear and why I am defining the 1st April as a certain watershed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand where are you going but it doesn't answer my question with respect to Mr. Hadzic specifically. Are you suggesting that after the 1st of April, his views changed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His views did not change because his views were different up to the 1st of April. His opinions never changed, at least this is what I could conclude from my conversations with him. Therefore, he could not change. He always remained the same. He was always a well-meaning and peace-loving person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So why does it say in your statement "until the 1st of April, he was in the moderate wing"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We defined the 1st of April as the day that I've just spoken about. Maybe the story about that event in temporal terms is something that was imposed on me, i.e., to start thinking about the time before the 1st of April and after the 1st of April. In the heads of the people who didn't change, including his head, means that he couldn't change. He was always the same, always equally well-meaning, always equally peace-loving.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come back to this topic a little bit later but I would like to ask you to place your mind back to June 1990 when you joined the SDS. Is it correct to say that at the time you were a professor of law at the faculty in Osijek, at the law faculty?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you were one of the founding members of the SDS in the Slavonia Baranja region?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A found -- a founder. I did found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at the time you had the trust of the party's leader, Dr. Jovan Raskovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as a trusted member of the SDS, you were allowed to meet with members of the Croatian government led by the HDZ in Zagreb. We saw a document earlier about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was only after a decision was made and after I got the green light from the highest body of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as a trusted member of the SDS, did you feel that as a representative of the Serb people you had very large responsibilities on your shoulders in dealing with the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And these meetings you had with the Croatian government were reported in the press, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document before we go on break. It's 65 ter 6576.1, at tab 3, please. You will see it appear on your screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is an article which was published in Vijesti, if that the name of the newspaper --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is actually Vjesnik. It was a Croatian daily at the time. Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise at least the three individuals we see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise them, of course. I'm the first on the left without hair. Next to me, Boro Savic. And, on the right, Ivan Vekic. The last was the representative of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you familiar with Mr. Vekic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I need to tell you this. Mr. Vekic was born in the same year as myself. Mr. Vekic and I attended the same grammar school in Osijek. He was in one class, I was in another class, for five years from grade 4 to grade 8. And obviously when we sat at the table and started talking, Vekic started by saying, "Gentlemen, Vojo," - that's me - "and I were classmates." We cannot address each other in second person singular. For a number of years we were -- we have been on first-name terms. Don't think that if we continue addressing each other that way that we are both corrupt. In other words, I know him perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And the other individual here is Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I just noted one error in the transcript. It is in line 8, page 24. It is "in second person singular." I think that is should be "second person plural."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And very quickly before the break, the other person we see on the screen is Mr. Savic. This is the man that you called an altar boy on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I don't know whether the connotation is the same in the Serbian language, but labelling someone an altar boy is not necessarily casting someone in a positive light. Is that the same in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those who come from mixed environments know what the meaning of the altar boy is. Those serve in church. Mr. Raskovic told me, "Don't go on your own to talk to the HDZ. Don't go on your own because unpleasant things can happen to you like they did to me when I had spoken to Tudjman. Takes one of our men with you and choose whoever you want." That's how I chose Boro Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We'll continue this after the break. And when we come back, I'd ask you to focus on your answers because you did tell us that during your examination-in-chief. So to make sure that we can finish as quickly as we can, just give me directly the answer. We will carry on after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe this is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, let me pick up where we left off. Again, we still have the picture on the screen. I was asking you whether this term you used with respect to Mr. Savic had a pejorative connotation. Were you in [Realtime transcript read in error "contact"] conflict with this man, Savic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps just to answer my question on that point. Is the term "altar boy" in the way that you used it meant to be pejorative?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was not pejorative. I don't mean to denigrate his role or to underestimate it. He had an important role because he was providing me with moral support, and I felt better in the company of the person whom I chose than without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you see in line 3, page 26, I don't know whether the witness -- the Prosecution used the word "contact".

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Conflict. "Conflict" was the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it correct to say that the newspaper article we see on the screen was issued, was it, the day after the talks you held with Mr. Vekic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3246, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, during this meeting on the 30th of August, you submitted a number of proposals and we saw them earlier this morning. I'd like you to take a look at these proposals. The version we have is 65 ter 6576. It's at tab 3 of the Prosecution's list. Now, this morning I used the word "original." Perhaps you can help the Trial Chamber understand. What is this version that we have on the screen here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left is the text that I typed on a typewriter, an Olympia. I used my private mechanical typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I take you down to item number 3. Here you're denouncing the use of certain terms such as rebels, highwaymen, Chetniks and other abusive terms when referring to Serbian people. Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it in the newspaper article, but I also know it from the text on the left-hand side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So it would be appropriate to say that you were not in favour of the use of such terms at the time that you typed this document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you advocated against the use of such terms against all people, of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely. It was not a time when brigands or highway robbers were coming in force, nor were we such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, for example, one term that was quite in fashion at the time was the use of the word "Ustasha," wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how did you feel about the use of that term?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha was a term used for the Croatian people. I could not feel offended by it myself, except that I found it ugly, no matter who was using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You say that the term was used for the Croatian people. In general?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is pejorative, offensive, negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And now I'd like to take you to item 4, which I believe might be on the next page in both Serbian and English. Yes, at the top of the page. And here you write that: "We propose that the use of the term 'armed rebellion' be stopped because the gathering of armed individuals is organised with the aim of self-defence and self-protection and thus does not constitute an armed rebellion ..." The question I have for you is here which gathering of armed individuals were you referring to? And this is August 1990.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were already days and events that brought unrest among the Serbian people because they were informed and it really happened that the Croats, through their special forces which already existed, including the Home Guards Corps, and they had weapons that been imported already in 1990 and these weapons found their way to irresponsible people, the Serbs believed that such people would be prepared to attack them using those weapons so they got ready to defend themselves. I sent a telegram to the chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army, asking that the parts of the Serbian people who were considered as the reserve force of the JNA - because all of us were reservists of the JNA - should have uniforms and weapons distributed to them because we shouldn't worry ourselves how to get hold of weapons. And thus equipped with regular uniforms of the reservists of the JNA and with weapons received from the army, they would be able to defend themselves, if necessary. And it was necessary in certain communities where certain forms of violence were already happening. Was I clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, but you mentioned a telegram to the General Staff of the JNA. Do you remember when you sent that telegraph -- telegram?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but that was a time when the first serious unrest began. I'm sorry, I can't remember the time. I thought it was legal. In my eyes, it was legal because we were the reserve force. We were in the reserve of a regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In any event, this would have been before you wrote this letter, the telegram that you sent?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I move on, Your Honours, this the document that we were discussing with Mr. Zivanovic. We could tender it at this time. 65 ter 6576.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, you were mentioning that leadership of the SDS, some members at least of the SDS, were in favour of talks and negotiations. Would it be correct to say that however this position may have been, there were elements at least in Krajina which were beginning to establish self-rule in areas inhabited predominantly by Serbs? And in terms of time-frame I'm talking as early as June of 1990. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such information, especially as far as June 1991 was concerned. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the establishment of the Community of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika on the 27th of June, 1990, by Mr. Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the 25th of July, 1990 declaration on sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people in Croatia which is also authored by Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the declaration had been adopted. It was on the 25th of July in a place called Srb, in Lika. It was a large gathering of Serbs, but I was indisposed at that time. I could not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are these the first steps towards self-governance by the Serbian people within the Republic of Croatia, at least as far as the Krajina area is concerned?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what the people who were doing it were thinking because I didn't speak to them. But thinking about this event and looking back, I believe those were the first attempts at self-governance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And through your interactions with the representatives of the HDZ and the Republic of Croatia, were you aware of how they received such initiatives or how they reacted to them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They received them with a lack of understanding and with serious objections that what was going on was not good and they didn't support it. They wanted themselves to create a legal framework for our activity. They wanted a legal framework of their own design. I don't know what that legal framework was to be, but the Serbs were very offended that they had been deleted from the constitution, that they were no longer a constituent people in Croatia, whereas they had contributed to the creation of Croatia as an anti-Fascist state. It was a great insult to the Serb people and threat to their existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you say "threat to their existence," would you agree with me that looking at the constitution of 1990, putting aside the fact that Serbs were removed as a constituent people, the rights of minorities were preserved in the constitution. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with that. They recognise Italians, Hungarians, Ruthenians, Slovaks, as minorities but not the Serbs. Even today when you drive through Croatia, you will not see a single sign in Cyrillic. And those Cyrillic signs that existed had been removed but there are signs in all the other languages. So you could say that minorities have rights, but why don't Serbs have any?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't going to delve into this, but I have the constitution before me and Serbs are listed as minorities. I can display it for you, if you wish. But are you saying, just so I understand your answer, are you saying that Serbs were not listed as minorities in the constitution or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. I know. The way in which they were introduced as a minority and the way in which they are referred to in the constitution of 1990 is not remotely similar to the way they were referred to before. You get the impression that in this union of peoples, the Serbs already have their place but it's wrong. I know what sovereignty means. Sovereignty is a legal term for violence. If you are not sovereign, you cannot decide your own fate in the same way as when you have sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me move on to a slightly different topic because earlier you mentioned that you sent this letter to the General Staff with respect to the arming of the reservists. Is it correct to say that in the fall or autumn of 1990, the SDS leadership from Croatia was seeking support from the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, too, was at that meeting with the Presidency of the SFRY when Borisav Jovic was the president of that Presidency. We were invited and we came there to describe the situation on the ground and the sentiment, the prevailing sentiment among our people. Depending on the speaker and their education, the descriptions varied, but all of them spoke about the fear from the new state and they had in common the desire to preserve Yugoslavia. Borisav Jovic, who was president of the Presidency, did not make any promises, did not say anything was black or white. He just listened and listened, and I don't know what he conveyed to others of our proposals. All I know is that the state of emergency was not imposed and one member of the Presidency who was to vote for it did not vote for it, and he was a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's take this one by one. You said: "I, too, was at that meeting." Just to clarify it for the Trial Chamber, when did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was September 1990. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you wrote -- you said here that "the Presidency invited us." Who was invited to attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prominent activists of the Serbian movement from Croatia. Better known individuals from all over Croatia, from Vukovar to Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I go on, I see here that your first answer at page 32, line 5, reads "At that meeting with the Presidency of SFRY when Borivoje Savic was the president," I think it's the name "Borisav Jovic" which was said.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borisav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And could you tell us some of the names of these prominent activists who were present at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Dzakula. Several people from Knin; I can't remember the names. I don't want to enumerate them now because my memory has faded, and my head is full of new people and new memories that pushed out the old one ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dusan Vjestica present?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was Mr. Goran Hadzic present?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You're not entirely sure?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we quickly display 65 ter 6577, at tab 5 in the Prosecution's list. And for the purposes of the version in B/C/S, could we zoom in to the top left-hand corner. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this is the 4th of October, 1990, a newspaper article called, "Which Serbs Went To See Jovic." And you see all the names listed there. Does that refresh your memory a little of who else attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, and I remember now when I see the names, that these people whose names were published in the newspaper were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you just maybe clarify for us. Earlier you said that you were invited by the SFRY president, Mr. Jovic. How did this invitation come across? Was it first initiated by yourself or did Mr. Jovic invite this delegation on his own initiative?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initiative was not mine. That's all I know. I don't know whom Jovic invited. I was invited by my friends and acquaintances who, at that time, lived in Belgrade. I don't know the other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3248, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Vukcevic, this was not the first --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe that's what I said but never mind.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said "Vuckovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise if I did. Now, Dr. Vukcevic, would you agree that this was not the first contact made with Mr. Jovic, with Mr. Borisav Jovic, at the time by Serbs in Croatia, or the Serb leadership in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were any contacts, I don't know anything about them. Nobody ever told me about them. Nobody ever invited me to be present either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the Serbian National Council from Knin during the summer of 1990?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't attend any meetings because I was not a member of the Serbian National Council. They were very selfish. They were a very closed group. They hid from the others, from the other members, as far as I can remember, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, which is minutes of this Serbian National Council. It's Exhibit P1195, at tab 1 of the Prosecution's list. Now, what you will see on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could we go to page 2 for both documents, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It might be a bit of a challenge for you because these are handwritten notes, but I'll ask you to make a bit of an effort, if I may. The header says here "Minutes" and from the 2nd session of the Serbian National Council, held on the 16th of August, 1990 in Dvor na Uni. Item 1, are you able to see item number 1 which starts with: "Milan Babic submitted a report ..."?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that there are letters on the screen, but not very legible. I can't read anything. Now I can, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The sentence that I'm looking at in English reads: "Milan Babic submitted a report about the talks with Borisav Jovic held by Babic with Raskovic and Bogoljub Popovic ..." Do you see that sentence? Do you see the sentence, Dr. Vukcevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And one sentence -- we skip one sentence here. The next sentence begins with: "Jovic gave support to all political battles for the rights of the people and that the referendum be led under the legal regulations and that the army will support and protect the political battle of the Serbian people." Do you also see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of this position by Borisav Jovic with respect to the support to the Serbian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that Borisav Jovic said something of that kind. When I met with him and when I was with the group of people that we mentioned a while ago, he didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in both English and B/C/S, and could we scroll down to item number 4. Actually, in B/C/S, it's the very next page. Yes, could we zoom in to item number 4, in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, here the translation that I have says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Demirdjian --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- turn over the page in English as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, it's the very bottom of that page, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, okay. It's only that one sentence. Sorry. We can go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, item number 4, as it is translated in English here, says: "Legal council. The president of the legal council - Vukcevic, unanimous." Do you have any idea as to what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were not many renowned legal professionals, especially full-time university professors but me in the ranks of the Serbian movement. And when I was chosen and elected and I was barely aware of that - I'm trying very hard to remember the whole thing - they tried to give me more significance to that position. Although I was in charge of the plebiscite which took place on the 19th of August, this was as much as I did as the president of the legal council. That was my only role, the only significant role that I had in the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And if we turn to page 6 in the English version and the next page in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is a list of those people who were present at this meeting of the Serbian National Council. And under number 16, we read: "Vukcevic Vojislav, MD, from Beli Manastir." Does that refresh your memory that you were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at several meetings in Knin. I can't remember whether this was a meeting of the Main Board or whether that was the meeting that is mentioned here. I really can't remember. It was a long time ago, first of all; and second of all, as I've already told you, I went there on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, earlier when I showed you the newspaper article which was entitled, "Who Went To See Jovic," you said that at the time Mr. Jovic did not react much. Would you agree that with time Belgrade did support the activities of Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that. Belgrade thought that it was their duty for national reasons because we did not have another state. We did not have any other assistance and help by any other Serbs but the Serbs who were in Belgrade. And they thought and felt invited to help us when they start feeling that way. I can give you an example when the Serbs from Belgrade did not help the Croatian Serbs the way that they expected, and that was on the 3rd of March, 1991, when Dzakula started a rebellion in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that eventually Belgrade started exerting pressure on some members of the SDS in your region?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade sent its commissioners and envoys to place under their control the Serbian people who had gathered and rallied in that way. The trouble with that was that those envoys and commissioners usually found and selected bad people, bad Serbs, and they failed in achieving what they had set out to achieve with the help of such bad people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. Out of the list that is on the screen, I would like to know whether number 16 -- well, we can see number 16, "Vukcevic Vojislav, MD." Is it the same person as the witness? And what does "MD" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is me but I'm not a physician. I'm not an MD.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you don't have any idea as to why the letters MD are indicated there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So this is a mistake. It is a mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will clarify this with the witness because I think that there is a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [In English] Sir, in the original version, we see your name, first of all, we see number 16, your last name. It is followed -- is it followed by the letters "DR" in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I am a doctor of science. I'm a doctor of law, not of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We'll revise this translation, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I was going to ask you about these commissioners you said which were sent from Belgrade. Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few of them have died, and as dead, they are not important. As for the rest, I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct that Mr. Ilija Koncarevic would be one of those commissioners who was sent to the region?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And would Mr. Ilija Petrovic also fit within this category?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this issue, I'd like you to take a look at an article in the Borba, which was published in Borba, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is at 65 ter 6606 at tab 13. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the original of this clipping is in English, as it was reported in the international press. The article is entitled: "The Strength and Weakness of Reasonable People." It is dated the 5th of April, 1991, and it talks about recent talks with Dr. Franjo Tudjman. And then the second paragraph here mentions your name. It says that: "Dr. Vojislav Vukcevic ... adds that the centre of power, Belgrade, has been exerting strong pressure on him because he influences the Serbs in Baranja to act calmly and responsibly and not to cause incidents." Does this accurately reflect words you would have used at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the time of this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: 5th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I owe it to tell that you I resigned from all positions in the Serbian Democratic Party on the 24th of April, 1991, and I parted with people whom I liked and others whom I didn't, and some I have never met after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will actually get to your resignation in a minute. But before that, I wanted to confirm with you that you held the view at that time that Belgrade had been exerting strong pressure on individuals like you who were trying to influence Serbs to keep calm in the Baranja region.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If on the term "Belgrade" you mean Milosevic's regime, then I have to say that people who represented him were not naive and they made sure who they spoke to and how they behaved. I can't say that pressure was put on me because I was already getting on. I had an integrity that they couldn't influence. They were in pursuit of some other more -- less stable people, I suppose, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You claim that: "The Serbian Democratic Party has split into two parts which do not acknowledge each other, and the influence of the Krajina part can also be felt in Slavonia and Baranja." Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I move to tender this exhibit Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to the issue of your resigning from the party, Dr. Vukcevic. In your statement, you say that you left the party because you were accused of being too soft. In fact, I'd like you to comment on an article that came out at the time in the Nin magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 6582 at tab 16 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Have you seen this newspaper article before, doctor? I believe you have it in front of you. Yes, very well. And do you remember giving this interview to the journalist Momir Ilic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the first question in the English version is at the bottom of page 1, and I think for you it's at the bottom of the first column. The question is here: "What prompted you to resign from all these positions in the SDS?" And here your answer is: "I'm doing this under the pressure of lies, defamation and all kinds of fabrications to which I have been exposed for the past five months." And you associate these or you attribute these lies and defamations to the Association of Serbs of Croatia based in Belgrade. Dr. Vukcevic, do you know who was the head of this association?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten his name; however, sometime in 1998 that man visited me. The man hails from Osijek, just like I do. I can't remember his name. And I spoke to him in a very serious manner, in a very decisive manner, and I told him that he had played a very ugly and dishonourable role on behalf of the Serbs. He swore that that was not true. And that would be my memory of the leader of the Association of Serbs from Croatia in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether a retired general by the name of Dusan Pekic had any role in that association?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was that role?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role that I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I see. And do you know whether General Pekic had any relationship with Mr. Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The next question here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is on page 2 in the English version; in the Serbian version it would be in the second column.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The next question is here: "It is being claimed that the SDS has been divided into two streams almost from its beginning and that the conflict between these two streams is still ongoing." And you explain here two forms of consciousness that prevail amongst the SDS members. Can I conclude from reading this article that the distinction between these two streams are between those members of the SDS who favoured dialogue and negotiations versus those who championed activism and possibly the use of force?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be more or less the main characteristics of the two streams, or the two parts, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, I will ask you to now look at a different interview, this time from 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 6601, tab 45 of the Prosecution list. It's an article in Vreme magazine, and the headline is, "Unlearned Lessons." I'll wait for the English version to come up on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this interview, Dr. Vukcevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember what I said during that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll walk you through it. The first section here deals with your resignation from all functions in the SDS, and you explained when that happened. And you explain some shortcomings and your astonishment at the time, and you referred to people who lied and people who believed those lies. This is -- the question here is: "Could you describe those people and events in more detail?" Do you see that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, we may have to move the original version. This is the third question, so it would have to be on page 2, please, of the B/C/S version. Yes, on the right -- on the left side of the screen, that's the question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If you can take a moment to read that answer, the answer you gave here. In the first section here, you mention: "Among them there were plain activists from the government --" sorry, "from the movement as well as people who came to visit us and took care of us, if you want, even the highest ranking person in this nation and the people who were closest to him, all of them repeating one and the same thought which at the time went as follows: All Serbs in a single state." Now, sir, when you said "the highest ranking person in this nation," you were referring to President Milosevic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your answer carries on here. You say: "My attempts to get from them a more concrete definition of that state regarding its size, its borders and national structure, remained fruitless because the protagonists and activists who promoted this idea were not able to explain it fully." And then you continue saying: "The task of the activists was to keep on repeating this idea they had learned by heart. The fulfilment of that idea and everything connected to it was supposed to follow only at the later stage and that task was to be assigned to some other people and activists. That is why I believe that some of those names, some of which I have forgotten, do not deserve attention. Unfortunately those names became our big misfortune." Sir, who did you have in mind with respect to those people who became your big misfortune?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
