utterances.text: For example, the president of the Association of the Serbs of Croatia, whose name I couldn't remember, and then also the late Dusan -- oh, well. Maybe I will remember his family name later. I can't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If it comes back to you, feel free to tell me at that moment. However, what is it that made them your biggest misfortune? What is it that they did?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did so much evil. They caused so much evil that it remains living to this very day, and God knows how long it will go on living and whether it will ever die.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you give us, in practical terms, what is the evil that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no country where you were born where you lived. The only country you thought was ever possible. Could there be any bigger evil than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to another part of this interview for one last question you were asked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the English version, we need to go to page 3, and in the Serbian version we stay on the same page but could we go to the middle column. Yes, right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Here the question is - and may I remind you this is an interview in August 1996 - "How do you see the future of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?" You answer here is saying that: "Since the beginning of current events, there was an idea for which I never had much understanding. It says that you must ask for more in order to get less. However, the problem isn't the fact that these people do not know what they want and when they're offered something, they do not know how to take it. I'm afraid that tackless statements and actions of Goran Hadzic and the leadership in Eastern Slavonia are simply repetition of what happened to Serbs in Krajina." Now may I ask you, Dr. Vukcevic, what are these tackless statements you referred to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember these statements now, and I remind you again of the fact that I stopped to think and to speak and to meet with people after I resigned. They lived in one area. I lived in another. All of us had our own problems, and I really can't remember now what I was thinking then and what these statements ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps whether these are statements that were made during or after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe for the answer on this question, the witness should have an opportunity to read this text to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fair enough. We can keep scrolling down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Dr. Vukcevic, I will leave this to Mr. Zivanovic to raise it in re-examination as I have more material to go through at this stage, if you don't mind. Because if we scroll to the next question - and that's on the very right side, thank you - here it says you are one of the Serbian politicians who actively negotiated with Dr. Franjo Tudjman and his associates before the war. "How did those negotiations start and what was their result?" Your answer here explains the release of 450 Serbs who had taken part in the events of the 3rd of March, 1991, in Pakrac, and you referred to that earlier this morning. And you carry on and you explain that you maintained a dialogue with Mr. Slavko Degoricija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe that to see this, we have to -- no, we can remain on this same page in the B/C/S version, scroll all the way to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The very last sentence begins with: "As we were satisfied with the results with President Tudjman we continued talks ..." and here we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S version. "We continued talks with Degoricija ..." And you explain here your talks with Mr. Degoricija and that he had offered to solve issues relating to the Serbs in Croatia, including constitutional status, economic relations, and cultural and educational matters. And you explain here the reaction of Serbs in Croatia in the following words. You say here: "Unfortunately, the Serbs did not accept this offer. Unfortunately, on that day, a group of feeble-minded and aggressive individuals from Baranja made itself heard and broke unity of the Serbian movement." If we skip a sentence you then say: "Several days later, the Serbian National Council passed a decision about separation of this region from Croatia and by doing so, became the first one, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that broke Yugoslavia. That evening, at this very session they passed a decision that professor Vojislav Vukcevic is not authorised any longer to speak on behalf of the Serbian people." Dr. Vukcevic, does this answer accurately represent your answers at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does. But there were worse statements and even worse happenings than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll get to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender this article, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned "worse statements and even worse happenings at that time." Would it be correct to say that at the time threats were made against you by individuals such as Vojislav Seselj and Jovo Ostojic? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially Jovo Ostojic and a man called Paroski from Vojvodina were throwing their weight about and competed who would find a worse name to call me and denigrate my work more. Can I explain just one more detail? Coming back from Zagreb after talking to President Tudjman, I turned on my car radio to Radio Belgrade because it was time for the news bulletin, and then quite unexpectedly I heard the speaker saying, "Our correspondent from Beli Manastir informs us that negotiations were just held in Zagreb between a representative of the Serbs and the Croatian president, Tudjman. The Serbian team included Mr. Vukcevic about whom we insist on saying that he is not a representative of the Serbs and has no authorisation to negotiate anything," although they knew about the decision authorising me. It was so ugly that I didn't know what to do. What can you do in that situation if you want to fight and do good and you are rejected by people? Can you imagine it? We hadn't even reached home. We were coming back from Zagreb, we were still on the highway, and we hear the voice on the radio saying these things about us. Of course, the people at that radio station were under the influence of the Belgrade regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. I apologise. My attention was attracted to the very next item I was going to show you at this moment. Sir, before I move to that, these words that were uttered against you were made during a rally in the village of Jagodnjak in April 1991, and I would like you to take a look at the footage that we have now in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can play the first clip which starts at the -- sorry, I must announce also the 65 ter number, 4785, at tab 17.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We haven't got it yet. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. For the interpreters, the first clip will not have any translation or any sound or any words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we play the first clip which is about 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can pause that here. You see the date on the screen which is the 21st of April, 1991, Dr. Vukcevic. I'd like to us go to the second clip, which starts at the 4 minutes and 10 second mark, and this is from page 1 of the transcript for the interpreters. Bottom of the page where you see the initials "V" and "Sh." If the interpreters want to give me the signal that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we play that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Brothers and sisters Serbs, the Serbian people of Serbian Slavonia, Western Srem and Baranja have made a decision through their Serbian National Council to join the present Republic of Serbia directly. This decision of the Serbian people is incontestable and has met with acclamation and support throughout Serbdom in general."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, did you hear Mr. Seselj here saying that this decision was brought through the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on the 21st of April, were you aware of who was the president or the head of the Serbian National Council?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give it any thought because I knew that whoever the president was, he was not defending his own opinion or policies. They got their opinions from elsewhere. Seselj was the chief person for Slavonia and Baranja and all that area, "of all the Serbdom," as he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, is this the appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Thirty-minute break. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, if I take a few minutes for planning purposes, I take you still can finish with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I could try, Your Honours, as much as I can. There may be a small spill-over into tomorrow morning, but I'll try my best to shorten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To discuss the next two witnesses: One is a closed-session witness, I think, and one is a public-session witness. Is that right, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next witness is for the public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's for the public session. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the witness after him, I must double-check, but I think also that he is for the public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The next witness there's no problem. It's Mr. Seselj; right? Now, it's about that witness that we might a problem. I saw your last e-mail, Mr. Zivanovic, about the problems you have with the Detention Unit. Is the second witness available? Would he be available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Second witness or the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the next witness after Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He arrived, but I don't believe he is -- he is ready to enter courtroom tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, because I will think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But, anyway, we can start with the next witness after this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we can start with Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Disregarding some problems that we met with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which then you will solve during the time Mr. Seselj is on the stand; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. We can bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a request, with your leave. I would kindly ask that we finish today, if at all possible. I need to return tomorrow because I am to attend a very important trial on Wednesday, and I would appreciate it very much if we could speed up a little and finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll try my best to restrict my questions to the essentials, Your Honours. I don't know if there's any re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course, the re-direct. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, we have re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll check whether we can have one extra session this afternoon, just in case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, of course --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're welcome, Mr. Vukcevic. And, of course, the length of your answers are of some importance now as well, aren't they? Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, just before the break, you were answering my questions with respect to a video we saw on the screen with Vojislav Seselj referring to the Serbian National Council, and I asked you whether you knew who the president was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask that we display on the screen, 65 ter 1D02959. This is at tab 14 of the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The article will appear on the screen in front of you, Dr. Vukcevic, and -- okay. We're having some problems with the monitor here. Do you see the article in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There we are. Okay. It's at the bottom right-hand corner - yes, that's what it is. The article is entitled: "Negotiations About Negotiations." And for your information, Dr. Vukcevic, it is dated the 10th of April, 1991, and it was published in Vecernje List. Could you confirm that this is a Croatian daily; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the first paragraph starts with "Vukovar." "After two relatively calm days, the population of the Vukovar district is attentively expecting the negotiations that should commence today in the municipal assembly of Vukovar." And towards the end of this first paragraph, we can see here: "Goran Hadzic, one of the leading SDS persons for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as well as the president of the so-called Serbian National Council, also announced that negotiations would last long." Now, this is the 10th of April, 1991, and the video we saw earlier with Mr. Seselj was 11 days later, the 21st of April, 1991. Would you agree that at the time Mr. Hadzic's role in the SNC was publicly available?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that the public read this and other newspapers that mentioned it, that covered it, to that extent, the public was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, of course, I was not there at the time you were. Can you tell us if this information at least was known to you in April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The fact that Mr. Hadzic was the president of the Serbian National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard people say that, the people around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, I'd like to show you a document, which is at tab 11. This is 65 ter 1939.13. At the very top, we see here: "At the session that took place on 17 March 1991 in Sid, National Council of Serbs has elected for the council chairman, Mr. Goran Hadzic, from Pacetin." The document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just object because this document, the translation of this document is not complete; namely, the footnote of this document was not translated. And in the original, if we can scroll down a little bit, we see the footnote reads -- it is too small. [Interpretation] "The decision was drafted after the session of the Great National Assembly of 25 June 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We can ask for a revision of the translation to include the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, this is a decision which was published in a book which was prepared by Mr. Ilija Petrovic himself, and it shows a date here, 17th of March, 1991. Would this appointment at this position in the Serbian National Council correspond to the time-period where the Serbian National Council was created?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was excommunicated very early on from many events because they harboured and fostered mistrust towards me. So there are many things I do not know. You have to believe me. It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we MFI it at this moment until we have an updated translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let if be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 3252 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just tell that I would object if it had to be tendered into evidence because the witness said that he doesn't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps it would be better to solve this immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- with your answer to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, we saw an article just earlier which showed that Mr. Hadzic's appointment to the Serbian National Council was in the public. This one gives us a more precise date of his appointment. Dr. Vukcevic told us a few minutes ago that he was aware, that at least by April 1991 Mr. Hadzic was holding this position. So this document, we would suggest, provides you a more precise date, and other excerpts from the -- Mr. Petrovic's book have been tendered through Mr. Hadzic's testimony, at least four of them. So this is another one of those decisions published in this book. So it is strictly for the sake of precising [sic] the date of his appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there is no foundation for the tendering of this document with this witness, this particular witness, and in particular because of the footnote was not translated and from which we can see that in the written form this decision did not exist before June, 25th of June, 1991. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps putting aside the footnote issue which we agreed we would translate, the witness just said a moment ago that he was familiar with the fact that at least by April Mr. Hadzic held this role, and it is publicly published in newspaper articles as well. So I think that there is a nexus to the witness. It showed that not only did he know at the time but here we have a more precise date in this document. And perhaps I could -- there's four exhibits that have been tendered so far from this book which have been shown to be reliable and which have been shown to actually connect to evidence about the events at the time. These are Exhibits P3214, P3215, 3216, and 3217.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the tendering of the other documents from this book have nothing to do with the tendering of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to say something and supplement my testimony by saying that, first and foremost, I did not respect either Petrovic or Koncarevic because in my mind the two of them were people who were not worthy of anybody's respect. Second of all, that was a time when you couldn't know what was information and what was just the opposite or misinformation. People say whatever they wanted, whatever pleased them, whatever suited them, and then they tried to convince you that they told you the truth, and then some other days you would hear the exactly opposite thing. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Vukcevic. Sorry. We are dealing here with a technical matter so just give us a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. So the document stays MFI'd until we have a translation with the footnote. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, I would like us to return to the video that we were looking at of the rally at Jagodnjak. If you remember earlier I mentioned to you that there were some utterances made by Seselj with respect to you, and I would like us to take a look for a moment as to what was said during this rally. You will see it in front of you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And before we go on, I'd like to make sure that the interpreters have the transcript. This is 65 ter 4785, tab 17, and we'll need to turn to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] The Serbian people will never accept any confederal rearrangement of Yugoslavia. No confederation. The present authorities in Croatia hit on the idea to form in divisions, arguments and conflicts among the Serbs because they realised they cannot achieve anything against Serbs when they are united and harmonious. They can always find a few, a handful of Serbian traitors, like this Djuna Djukic, assistant to the Ustasha minister of police, who formed a new Serbian national party with the sole aim of introducing a Trojan horse into the Serbian ranks. That party will never have any success among the Serbian people. After all, in World War II, during a genocide in which 1 million Serbs were killed, the Ustasha leader Pavelic had a Serbian deputy, Besarevic. There will always be such traitors, but we shall always recognise them and brand them on time. "Here, among you in Baranja, another such traitor has appeared. It is Vojislav Vukcevic whom the Serbian people has already driven out. What is the aim of these traitors? Today they speak in favour of the cultural autonomy of the Serbian people in Croatia, but they also argue in favour of Croatia remaining within the borders given to it as a present by the criminal and crook Josip Broz Tito. The Croatian authorities are now willing to give the Serbs any form of autonomy - cultural, political, or territorial - anything the Serbs want, as long as they get a confederation in return. "What is their aim? The present internal borders in Yugoslavia are purely administrative and they are not protected by any norm of international law. We can change them at will insofar as our political strength allows, and the world does not dare interfere. If we agree to a confederation, these borders suddenly become borders between states, protected by the norms of international public law, and can never be changed again."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, you heard the term "traitor" being used when Mr. Seselj spoke of you. What impact did such speeches have on your life at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They caused revulsion, but I don't know what other people thought about either him or me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, sir, these type of speeches at the time made by Seselj and later on we'll see Paroski or Ostojic, didn't these speeches have a impact on their followers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You heard the clamour of the people who supported him. Those same people applauded me only a year earlier. This is the lot of the politicians everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So would you say that there had been a radicalisation of this population?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived with a mission and the mission was to do things the way he did them. Very few people were so skilled and successful at manipulating the people the way he did. And I'm sure that he had his supporters and like-minded people. You heard people applauding when he said that I was a traitor. I established the Serbian party in that same village, and I managed to put -- restore order among two factions in the same village. One faction were former Chetniks; the other, former partisans. And they applauded me when I did that, and only a year later, you heard what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did you hear also at the end of his speech Seselj seems to be challenging the established borders of the republics within the former Yugoslavia, and he challenges those borders drawn, as he says, by Tito. What did you think of such views at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally what I thought, I thought that it was too late, that things like that should have been said well in time and not when he said them; and that his only goal was not only to change the borders but also to create misfortune which appeared very soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender this video, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3253, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, were you familiar with the fact that after the rally was held at Jagodnjak the police from Osijek investigated the content of these speeches?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of rumours. A lot was written about things. I can't remember what happened because by then I had already been revolted by the whole thing, by all of the events, by some of the people. And I really can't remember what the Osijek police did, whom they questioned. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you familiar with or were you in contact with the police chief, Mr. Josip Reihl-Kir?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in contact with him but I can tell you why and when. The Serbs wanted me to supply them with arms. I said I didn't have any and that I couldn't give them any arms. And then I called an activist from our movement. I wanted the two of us to go after see the chief of police Kir. His name was Dragica Radic. He went with me. I came to see the chief of police and I told him what the Serbs required from me, and I asked him to come and meet with the Serbs and told them what was possible. And that's what happened in late February 1991. I brought him to a meeting of the SDS board for Baranja. I could have knocked them out with a feather when they saw whom I had brought to that meeting. They thought that it was a terrible provocation, that it was not possible. However, he was not just a common policeman. He was very extraordinary. He was very smart, very well-meaning, and he said, "I promise you" - and I have the minutes of that meeting - "I promise you you will get weapons if you apply for them but on one condition, not because you're Serbs or you're not Serbs. You just have to prove that you are not under criminal investigation, that there are no proceedings instituted against you. If not, you will get arms." And that's the same all over the world and Croatia is not an exception. That's how it was. Those who wanted to get weapons, or at least that's what I think, nobody complained or bragged about that. However, I heard that those who had applied did receive weapons. On that occasion, he also asked us try and influence those Serbs who were members of the police to come back to work because he personally promised them that nothing bad would happen to them if they would only come back to work. And when that tragedy happened to Kir, Serbs in Baranja used a slogan and that slogan was "No peace after Kir."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And very briefly could you please tell me, do you know whether he made a genuine effort at investigating those speeches made by Seselj, Ostojic, and Paroski, specifically threats that were made -- or words used against you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. However, I never doubted his good intentions or his goodness as a man. If it did not cost him anything, I mean in his position, I'm sure that he did it. He was a good man. That's how I saw him and perceived him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic, Dr. Vukcevic, and it relates to your testimony where you stated that -- and this was on Thursday of last week. You stated you met Goran Hadzic on the 9th of June, 1990, when the SDS border was created in your region, but you also said that you had met him before as his wife was a student.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. You also stated that you had met him before as his wife was a student of yours.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how frequent had you met Mr. Hadzic before 1990 and how close were you to him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were just chance meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just happened to meet him. We would greet each other. We would be polite and civilised when we happened to see each other, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Earlier this morning you mentioned that you -- I believe you said you knew his family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And by "his family," who did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the guests at his christening in 1990, on the 14th of October or 14th September or, rather, it was his patron saint's day, on Saint Michael's Day. And then I saw all of them in one place, his mother, his father, and all those who were his family members. They were decent people, ordinary, decent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And did you happen to entertain each other or invite one another for dinners?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were just the beginnings of our work in the Serbian Democratic Party. Later we did what we had to. Each day was more complex and more complicated than the previous ones. It brought new problems, new activities. We didn't socialise at that time. We would see each other at meetings and gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And following the 9th of June of 1990, did that relationship develop a little more?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did, insomuch as we travelled together to Knin. We attended the sessions of the Regional Board of the SDS, when we met on party business, on the business of the Serbian Democratic Party, and there was nothing else but that. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned last Thursday a discussion you had with Mr. Hadzic in relation to a speech given by a man named Kresojevic in Belgrade. You remember talking about that last Thursday?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you discussed this speech with Mr. Hadzic during a car ride to Knin, and I'd like to ask you if you remember approximately --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- when did this car ride take place.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after his speech in Belgrade. And that event was still fresh, very fresh in our memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And this event in Belgrade took place when.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was it in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I assume this would have been the second half of 1990.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand well, the substance of what Mr. Kresojevic said in his speech was that Serbs from Eastern Slavonia fully supported Milosevic. Is that what it was about?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if I look at your statement, you say there that: "Goran Hadzic said at the time that he would not make a speech supporting Milosevic..." Is that the gist of his reaction?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was it who was not going to speak in favour of Milosevic? Goran Hadzic or Milosevic? I didn't quite understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The sentence reads as follows: "Goran Hadzic said at that time that he would not make a speech supporting Milosevic on any account."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did he tell you why he considered it objectionable to support Milosevic? Did he explain that to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he believed that I shared his opinion, and we thought that the Serbs in Serbia did not understand the Serbs in Croatia and that they had a different view of the space, time, and people, the people's sentiment and desires. And although we were Serbs just like the Serbs in Serbia, in some historical moments, we were two entirely different worlds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that in doing so, Hadzic displayed a great deal of courage in telling you his position with respect to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- he never stated this position in public, did he?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he said, where he said it, whether yes or no. I don't know. I didn't follow the events so closely and so precisely, so I wouldn't know. I have to tell you, though, that the Serbs in Croatia differed and that they were distinguished into those who supported Milosevic and those who didn't. Milosevic was not supported by those who were better acquainted with the circumstances of the Serbs in Croatia because people who came from Serbia and who behaved in the way they did could not be supported. However, whoever did not praise Milosevic was not a good Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to take a look at an interview, Exhibit P1742. It's at tab 55. This is an article entitled: "Man For Tough Talk." It was published on the 25th of March, 1992, in Borba. And in the English version, I would like us to turn to page 3, and in the B/C/S version, could we go to the bottom of the second column. There's a question there put to Mr. Hadzic which reads as follows: "What is your position towards the SPS and Slobodan Milosevic?" Now, Mr. Hadzic gives a lengthy answer at the end of which he says the following. We have to turn to page 4 in the English version, and in the B/C/S version, we need to go to the top of the third column. Yes. There's a sentence here that reads as follows: "I have a good relationship with Milosevic for whom I believe ... is the greatest living Serb politician and I have great respect for his work ..." Now, Dr. Vukcevic, this is March 1992. Perhaps Goran Hadzic displayed some courage in a one-on-one conversation with you, but I would put it to you that he had great respect for Milosevic, just as he says publicly in this interview. Would you agree that this courage he displayed was only in private?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what he said, but I don't know what he was thinking when he said it. It's very hard to speak on somebody's behalf. It's very difficult to say what one person thinks when he says what he does. As I've told you, after the 15th or 20th of April, 1991, I excommunicated myself of my own will. I removed myself from everything that I had been doing up to then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I can imagine that as a founder of this political party, these were shocking moments in your life.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very, very.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in the same -- or in the same topic, if you remember at least in your statement, you state that up until April 1991, when you left the party, Hadzic was in the moderate wing of the SDS, and I asked you this morning if it meant that this changed. But you were not in touch with him anymore after you left the leadership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was no longer in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I want to show you a small clip which is dated January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P53 in Sanction, please. This is tab 9. For the interpreters, this will be page 1 of both English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Vukcevic, the clip I'm going to show you is on the occasion of the celebration of Sveti Sava, which I understand is held on 27th of January each other. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. 27 January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are the interpreters ready with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we show the first clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "Goran Hadzic: Brothers and sisters, I greet you with our traditional Serb greeting: May God be with you. "As president of the Municipal Board which you belong to, let me say, as it is my duty, a few words about our Vukovar Municipal Board. Even though there are many topics we're going to discuss later on, our party was established on 10 June last year in Vukovar and 19 boards have been established since then. Today the party has 21 boards and I congratulate you on establishing your two local boards. We have already faced many problems in our party. You are familiar with them and you know who caused them. However, we managed to overcome them and we should thank our current leadership ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted you to listen to this original portion of the clip which establishes the date when the local boards were created, and you've testified about that earlier. I'd like you now to look at the second clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And for the interpreters, we need to turn to page 2 in both of English and the B/C/S. The time code for this one will be 3 minutes, 29 seconds onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, while we're fixing some technical issues, can I ask you, are you -- were you present at this rally by any chance?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are the interpreters ready with page 2?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just waiting for the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "Goran Hadzic: For the moment we have to accept it and organise ourselves which you had occasion to see on the TV two nights ago. I'm sure that you experienced it just as I did. This is what I think. In the whole world we cannot find 80.000 Serbs who would just say something bad about another people, who would just verbally say something offensive about other people. Whereas, those others have 80.000 machine-guns in their possession and keep them so they could use them against us. It is ridiculous. 1941 has happened again. 1945 has happened again. Then in 1971, we thought we would forgive them. It wouldn't happen again. I'm telling you now, if the Croatian people do not renounce their Ustashas publicly, we will propose through our Serbian National Council that we cut all ties between Serbs and Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, would you able to hear what was said? I know the volume was not perfect but were you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is the 27th of January, and Mr. Hadzic here talks about 1941, 1945, and that the Croatian people should renounce their Ustasha. If you remember earlier today, we talked about these sorts of terms - Chetnik, Ustasha - being used around that time. Is this the type of speech you favoured at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not use these terms. But you have to understand the frame of mind that prevailed in that time. This is a typical moment when the masses expect you to say the words they are harbouring in their hearts and minds, traumatised as they were. To make a rapprochement with them and to convince them that you feel the same, sometimes you have to say even things you don't mean in order to be closer to them, and then they would accept you as one of their own, as one they hold dear. You should not take Goran Hadzic always at his word when you listen to his speeches. His speeches were tailored to the occasion in order to make him accepted by the crowd. We ourselves did not always feel comfortable in such places. Here and now, it is very difficult for you to understand the state of mind that prevailed among the people then. You can't understand what it was really like. When, in your own country, you cannot walk freely, you cannot speak freely, you cannot act like before, then you can hardly avoid the reaction of the kind you just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you tell us that while you were in the party leadership, "We kept appeasing the Serbs and telling them that the genocide of the Second World War would not be repeated." Now, sir, this speech we heard a moment ago - and this is a just a small clip; there is more - this speech we heard a moment ago clearly goes against your efforts to appease the Serb population, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been telling you things as I saw them but you must believe me that behind these words is a very sincere, open heart. It's not exactly as it sounds. Things are not as they appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But publicly to those who are in the gathering here and listening to his words, those words are not going to appease them, are they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, you can try to find peace and appease others, but when you get out of that place and you know that you will not be allowed to stay in peace, that somebody would raise a hand at you, would shoot at you, then you cannot be surprised at this sentiment among these people and that they wanted to hear words like this. They expected, they wanted to hear this, if I am at all good at reading people's emotions. It all depends on the educational attainment, on their personal experience, on their age, if they had already lived through something similar before, then they would be more sensitive, more receptive to these words. I've already told you that I was not very popular. My house was fired at. I was attacked. People didn't like me because I was telling the truth. People don't want to hear the truth. They want to hear what they wish for. And you have to be very careful in evaluating what is publicly said, what is actually meant. In Belgrade I gained some experience in politics and I learned one thing: People do not like the truth. They expect you to say the things they want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If I may cut you here so that we carry on. Dr. Vukcevic, it is correct, however, that would you not have made this speech?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not, but it doesn't mean that others would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: During this speech, which we just heard, he also makes a reference to the Serbian National Council which was created perhaps three weeks before this rally. You were not in favour of the creation of the Serbian National Council, were you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not because Serbs had their own national council based in Knin. And Milan Babic was president of that Serbian National Council, and we believed that they were some kind of Serbian shadow government and that one was enough. We didn't need another. However, there were people who made it happen, that another Serbian National Council be established for Eastern Slavonia as well, had certain purposes in mind. Goran Hadzic, who has in his life uttered many words which he didn't mean, is not the greatest culprit. You should not consider him as the greatest culprit. There are many others who are more responsible than he and who are no longer alive. I remembered, by the way, two names you asked me about before. One was Dusan Kulic, another was [Realtime transcript read in error "Milan"] Jovan Popovic, and a third one was Jovan Krkobabic. He died recently. He was the deputy prime minister of Serbia. He demanded that I follow their instructions; otherwise, I would not fare well and I indeed didn't fare well. So judge for yourself: Did Goran Hadzic say these things because he meant them or because he had to say them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, on the topic of the Serbian National Council, I'd like you to look at an interview you gave on the 15th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 6580, at tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I just think that one of the names was not transcribed correctly. It is in line 19. After Dusan Kulic, it was written Milan Popovic. But as far as I heard, the witness mentioned another name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, if you could specify --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Dusan Kulic, Jovan Krkobabic, and Jovo Kokot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We see here a newspaper article entitled: "New Serbian National Council Founded in Secret." This was published in Vjesnik on the 15th of January, 1991, and I'd like to take you to the third column in the B/C/S version and that's page 2 in the English version. Yes, we can scroll down a little bit for the B/C/S version. Thank you. I believe the title of this section is called "They Surprised the SDS," and it reads here: "Ilija Koncarevic was elected the Secretary-General of the Serbian National Council. However, it is unclear what this had to do with what is in Knin, but it is clear that the scenario of their actions is the same. However, its formation surprised even some of the responsible leaders of the SDS. Vojislav Vukcevic, the vice-president of the SDS Executive Committee, speaking about the current events in Croatia, called the council ... unconstitutional. In Vukcevic's opinion, if something was formed, it could only be a board of the already existing Serbian National Council formed in Knin." And if we scroll up in the B/C/S version all the way to the top of the fourth column, the following sentence says: "It is obvious that the Knin-ification of Slavonia and Baranja is starting ..." Now, sir, by calling or by stating that this council was unconstitutional, can you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant what is written and what I said. I said that the Serbs already had their Serbian National Council based in Knin and it was valid for all the Serbs in Croatia. I thought that every fragmentation and every separation of any part of Croatia from the whole amounted to a breakup of Yugoslavia, that it was contrary to the interests of Yugoslavia, and we were fighting to preserve Yugoslavia. That's why I was saying we don't need a national council for Slavonia and Baranja because we already have one national council based in Knin for all the Serbs, and that's exactly as we read here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Vukcevic, I heard you earlier when you stated that -- well, let me actually get the words exactly so I don't misquote you. You said that: "Goran Hadzic, who has in his life uttered many words which he didn't mean, is not the greatest culprit." Now, sir, whether he meant those words or not, he did say them and they did have an impact on the people on the ground; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not among the people on the ground, and I don't know what kind of impact it made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You didn't remain in Baranja until September 1991, however. That's what I mean by "on the ground."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but until the 6th of September, I had spent one year in the monastery of Hilandar, on Sveta Gora, the holy mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not very clear to me here. One year in a monastery?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only one month, but in that year, 1991, before I definitively left Beli Manastir. In fact, I was expelled from Beli Manastir. They had seized my car and told me that the staff of Baranja had made a decision that I had to leave. That was my activity for that year. And as for Sveta Gora and the monastery of Hilandar, I spent the entire month of July 1991 there. And then I returned briefly to Beli Manastir and then again I travelled again to Belgrade and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand that you have some sympathy for Mr. Hadzic. However, considering what you were trying to achieve, I'm putting it to you that you may have been a negotiator, someone who was ready to talk, but what we see here goes against your every effort, a creation of a Serbian National Council, speeches which are not aimed at appeasing the population, the use of terms that you did not condone, such as Ustasha and the like?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other side, the side that demanded it from Goran Hadzic, was much stronger than I. I was just an ordinary man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago that you were expelled from Beli Manastir and that they seized your car and told you that the staff of Baranja had made a decision that you had to leave. Was this staff led by a man named Borivoje Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was always a very small man and remained a small man. He was just an assistant to another Borivoje who was the commander of the Baranja Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the last name of this commander?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Dobrokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. Looking at the questions I have, I will probably need another 20 minutes. I'm not sure if we have made arrangements for an extra session to complete the witness's testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We did, Mr. Demirdjian. Mr. Zivanovic, your re-direct, time-wise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My estimate is half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will -- is this the time for you -- the best time for you to break?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, because I will enter a topic which will last more than two, three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will break now and come back at 3.00 for a one-hour session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I'll keep you to that, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very grateful to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're welcome, Mr. Vukcevic. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, I will try to go as fast as I can so we can complete your testimony this afternoon. So I'd like us to take a look at a document which is 65 ter 6588, at tab 44. And, Dr. Vukcevic, this is in line with the topic that we left off with respect to your role as a negotiator and the comparison we made with the words uttered by Mr. Hadzic in early 1991. What we have here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honours, we need to go into private session for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, before the break I did use a newspaper article which captured Dr. Vukcevic's reaction to the creation of the Serbian National Council but I failed to tender it. This was 65 ter 6580. May I move to tender it at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, after you left Baranja in September of 1991, you went to establish yourself in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that in early 1992, you started to work before the Belgrade Military Court?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this does not appear anywhere in your statement that we have here. Is there any reason why this was not included in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. However, to your question, I can only say that there was no reason for me not to include that. The supreme military prosecutor was my friend. He hailed from a village near Osijek. He offered me an opportunity and he told me, "You lost your job. I am offering you to be an attorney-at-law to represent the people who were arrested as members of the ZNG," the national guards in Croatia. "Defend them as much as you can and as much as you wish." That's how I became a defence counsel ex officio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, as a defence counsel, you represented, as you just said a moment ago, members of the ZNG. And may I ask you, first of all, what is the name of the prosecutor you were mentioning, the supreme military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miladen Papic. Unfortunately, he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: According to the information that I have found, you seem to have defended quite a few members of the ZNG; perhaps somewhere around 15 or 20. Would that be right or is it more than that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct to say that in some cases you did represent two or three accused in the same trial?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The most attractive trial for the most heinous of crimes had Cibaric as the accused, Nikola Cibaric. I also represented Ksenija Piplica and Marko, whose family name escapes me at the moment. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in none of these trials did you represent more than one defendant?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, during these -- during the time that you were working before the Belgrade Military Court, did you at any time represent any members of the JNA or SFRY armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I did represent a young soldier. I believe that he deserted from the JNA. He was a Croat from Zagreb. I represented him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Were there -- in fact, to your knowledge, were there any proceedings against JNA soldiers or members of the Serbian Territorial Defence for alleged crimes committed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I spoke to the prosecutor and his deputies - I'm referring to the late Papic - and I asked them how come you're only charging people with armed rebellion? It's a trivial crime when everything indicates that what they did was they committed war crimes. They were surprised by my question, but they were first and foremost surprised that I dared ask them that. They were not so much surprised with the essence of my question because they had read a lot and they knew a lot, and they knew that those crimes were war crimes, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to come back to my question, I was not asking about the qualification of the crime; I was asking whether there were any proceedings against not ZNG or Croatian defenders but against JNA and Serb TO defenders -- fighters. Do you know whether there were any proceedings against JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a case against a Serb who opened fire on another Serb for private reasons. However, the proceedings against him were not conducted in the same way the proceedings were conducted against the members of the ZNG, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned a moment ago the name of Nikola Cibaric who you represented before the military court. Were you informed by Mr. Cibaric about the circumstances of his arrest and his detention?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I don't remember what I heard from him, but the person was rather simple, retarded, that is. He had killed a woman, the mother of three children, on the order or at the request of another man who told him, "Bring the woman out and kill her." And so he did. At that time the prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was Milan Panic. He had been sent from the USA to conduct the Serbian policy. Cibaric was sentenced to death because death penalty was still part of the legal system. They were all sentenced to death. I was not able to defend them because the facts of the crime were uncontestable. Milan Panic, actually, exchanged them and returned them to Croatia, and he got several Serbian pilots in exchange for those men. I don't know who the pilots are; I never saw them. But I know that those people who had been sentenced to death were actually acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said a moment that you don't remember what you heard from him in relation to his arrest and his detention. If I were to put it to you that Mr. Cibaric was severely tortured, would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember whether he told me that or not. You know what? As I've already told you, he was of diminished mental capacities. I'm sure that he was under a lot of pressure in view of the fact of what he had done and what people did to him. He didn't know who I was, whether I was a proper defence counsel or whether I was sent to provoke him. I really can't remember whether he told me those things the way you say that he might have. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that the bulk of the evidence against him was a statement that he gave, that he provided to the military court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object to this line of questioning. We shall not review the proceeding -- criminal proceeding before the military court, and it is not in relation to this case at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not clear about the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zivanovic, could you clarify? Is it relevance? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This subject is completely irrelevant, how the military court of Yugoslavia worked in criminal proceedings against this particular person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is part of the -- well, maybe I shouldn't make these comments in front of the witness. Perhaps he should remove his headphones before I explain myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic? Mr. Vukcevic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then could I ask you to remove your headphones off for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, it is part of the Prosecution's case that the Yugoslav armed forces obviously were part of the joint criminal enterprise - that is what we are saying - and that the military judicial system was one-sided and that it was biased. This gentleman was in a position to give us some information about the functioning of the military judicial system. He has given us already an answer in saying that only one group of people or one side to the conflict were being tried by this military judicial system, and this is the line of questioning that has the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not informed that the military justice system of Yugoslavia was a part of joint criminal enterprise. It is first time that I hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's not what Mr. Demirdjian said. Mr. Demirdjian said JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: JNA, but these questions are about military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which are part of the JNA. We've heard the military expert extensively on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll allow the question, Mr. Demirdjian, if the question and answer doesn't take more than a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Much obliged. Let me go back to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Vukcevic, you can put back your headphones. Let me repeat the question, Dr. Vukcevic. Is it correct to say that in the Cibaric case, the bulk of the evidence against him was a statement that was -- that he provided to the military court?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the circumstances of how the statement was taken from him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: He didn't tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't remember. It was such a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let me show you one document, Dr. Vukcevic, and we'll conclude with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we show 65 ter 6600 at tab 43. We can go to page 5 in the English version and page 1 in the B/C/S version. That's fine. It appears that this topic was doomed from the beginning, so I will conclude my cross-examination at this stage. Dr. Vukcevic, I thank you for your answers this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Mr. Zivanovic, cross -- sorry, re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukcevic, I'd like us to look at a document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor, P3250. This is an interview in the Vreme magazine published on the 10th of August, 1996. I'm interested in page 2, both in the original and in the English translation. Only one part of interview was read out to you so you couldn't say what that part referred to. That's why I'm going to read the entire passage. The question was: "How do you see the future of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, i.e., the territory under the transitional administration of the United Nations?" Your answer was this: "At the beginning of all these developments from before, there was a thought for which I did not have enough understanding. It says that you must ask for more in order to get less. "However, the problem is in the fact that these people don't know what they want, and even when they are offered something, they don't know how to take it. I am afraid that tackless statements and actions by Goran Hadzic and the leadership in Eastern Slavonia are simply a repetition of what happened to the Serbs in Croatia while they lived in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. "The representatives of that people ought to know what they can ask for and how much they can ask for. The UN Security Council extended the Erdut agreement until July 1997 ..."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the year was 1997. It was, rather, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Could you please wait for me to finish and then I will invite your comments. Now I'll continue reading: "... and one should not expect that this dead-line will be extended any further. Therefore, in the remaining 12 months or less, they must adapt their demands not only to the mood of the other party to the agreement, that is Croatia, but also the interests of the international community which will not go back upon its word. The situation in Bosnia shows this clearly, doesn't it? Why is it that they cannot learn from their experience going back only a bit longer than a year ago? How come that they have not learned to ask for much in order to get less but to ask exactly as much as they can get? As much as they can get has already been written and signed by them in the Erdut agreement. Why do think now demand more than that? In whose interests are they doing that?" First of all, let me tell you that what you said was said in 1995.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us -- you were very critical but when was that? Was that after the war or during the war or, rather, was this happening during the period between 1991 and 1993? This what we are the most interested in.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was such an ardent advocate of the Z-4 plan which was offered to the Serbs by the international community. I thought that was the best for them. Let me use just a couple of words to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. I am only entitled to ask questions arising from the cross-examination by the Prosecution. Since the Z-4 plan was not a subject of their cross-examination, we have to limit ourselves to what I am entitled to ask.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you said that they were asking for more than they could get was precisely the Z-4 plan. The public in Serbia was in total upheaval and so over-excited over it that it's difficult to even imagine today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, was this a kind of criticism for rejecting the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That was the worst, the stupidest, the dumbest act of the Serbs from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just remember when the Z-4 plan was on the table?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. February 1995. The mass media in Serbia reported at that time that Milan Martic didn't want to take the Z-4 plan in his hands even. A man with modest education, almost without any education at all, had the right to reject a text that the most eminent legal experts have drafted and the most prominent diplomats brought to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at D184.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, you heard the question of the Prosecution whether the Serbian National Council ever adopted a decision to annex the region to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have this document now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the text "Vukcevic cannot represent us" in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are certainly able to read this.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I have my own copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here is my question then: We see here in the first sentence: "The Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, at its session last night, decided to annex these lands to Vojvodina," et cetera. When you spoke about the decision of the Serbian National Council to annex the region to Serbia, did you mean this decision?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I meant another decision. When I said that, I had lost sight of this fact, and you reminded me quite rightfully that I made a mistake. I should add to my answer. What else can I say? Stupidity and ignorance have no limits. They are immeasurable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were saying that the Serbian National Council had made a decision to join --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it sounded as if it was presided over by Goran Hadzic, but that's not true. By that time, he was already outside of the district.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at this text's date? When was it published?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This text says that the decision was made at the session the night before.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was one day after the meeting in Obrovac, on the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1742.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked you, among other things, whether in his public appearances Goran Hadzic ever spoke against Milosevic and he showed you this text. Could we look at the box with the subheading, "Monarchist, Royalist." I will read out to you only the first sentence. This is what Goran Hadzic says here: "I'm a royalist by conviction. But I accept the majority decision of the people who are to state their own views and wishes. It would be my wish for the people to vote for a monarchy, for the king to come back, but I would like to see a monarchy of the Swedish type." This is a quotation. How would this sound to the ears of President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the same as if a wasp got into his ear and buzzed inside. Milosevic could not stand the idea of a monarchy and he couldn't stand the people who were talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was there a certain degree of civil disobedience or courage for a political leader at that time to come out with something like this in public?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly civic courage, and he was taking great risks. And, after saying something like this, he could well expect anything to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P53. It is second page, both in original and English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor showed you a video-clip filmed at a rally in January 1991. I will not play it again, but I will read to you part of the text that was discussed. I believe it is in the record. Let me ask you first: Do you recall that some illegal distribution of weapons in Croatia was broadcast on TV in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that programme was seen by all of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out to you only one passage from what he said. Goran Hadzic says on page 2: "This is my thinking. In the entire world we could not find 80.000 Serbs who would just verbally come out against another people, whereas they have 80.000 automatic rifles and keep them in store to use them one day against us.
